Yubileiny: Russia’s Launch of an Experimental “Reactionless” Drive

In 2008 Russia  launched of the Yubileiny (Jubilee) educational microsatellite, which reportedly carried an experimental "reactionless" (or propellantless/inertial) drive for in-orbit testing.

The Experimental DriveIn 2009, Russian media (including outlets like http://Pravda.ru, http://Infox.ru, and others) reported that the satellite hosted a test of a so-called reactionless thruster—one that supposedly generates thrust without expelling any propellant or reaction mass, potentially defying classical conservation of momentum. 

The device drew power from the satellite's electrical system (around 6–8 W in some descriptions) and was linked to inventors/researchers like Spartak M. Polyakov (associated with a "vortex drive" using swirling mercury or fluid in conical/spiral paths to create asymmetric internal forces) and figures such as Valery A. Menshikov (from the Research Institute of Space Systems).

The claimed mechanism involved creating a "tornado-like" flow or non-equilibrium motion in a sealed system (e.g., via pumps and motors driving fluid in changing geometries), aiming to produce a net axial force, especially during transients like startup. It was sometimes nicknamed "gravitsapa" (a humorous/scoffing term from Russian media, evoking sci-fi perpetual motion gadgets).

Initial media hype in 2009 suggested tests (some reportedly in 2008–2009) were "encouraging" or "successful in general," with claims of orbital adjustments without propellant.

However, no verifiable orbital changes were observed. Critics, including Eduard P. Kruglyakov from the Russian Academy of Sciences' Commission on Pseudoscience, stated the device produced no measurable effect—"the thruster did not change the satellite’s orbit by even a micron."

Results were described as "mixed," "ambiguous," or outright null in orbit, despite possible bench artifacts or measurement errors on Earth. No detailed public data (e.g., thrust curves, Doppler residuals, or attitude logs) supported success.

Just so you know in advance, the Russian Academy of Sciences serves as cover up for all the technologies they are testing, while the military, as always, takes those technologies for its own needs.
